title: Steve Kerr: 'The Sonics Belong in Seattle'
htmlContent:
Steve Kerrhas never been shy about where he stands on the Seattle Supersonics. And with the NBA's expansion decision drawing closer, the Golden State Warriors coach made it clear once again that he wants to see the franchise back where it started.

Speaking in Seattle, Kerr was asked about reports that the city's expansion hopes have been used as leverage, both in the NBA's recent talk aboutMexico City and years ago when Phoenix was pushing for arena upgrades. Kerr kept his answer measured, but his message was clear.

"Business is Business"

Kerr admitted he was not familiar with the details of how Seattle has been used in those negotiations.

"I didn't know that, so it's hard for me to comment," Kerr said. "I do know that business is business, and people are going to try to drive business, whatever that means."

Then he got to the part that mattered most to Sonics fans.

"But I do know that the Sonics belong in Seattle," Kerr said. "And I think it would be wonderful to see them back, but I can't really comment on the detail within all that."

It was a careful response from a coach who knows the business side of the league is above his pay grade. But Kerr's stance on the bigger question has never wavered.

A Longtime Sonics Supporter

Kerr's support for Seattle goes back years. When the Warriors played a preseason game at KeyArena in October 2018, the first NBA game in Seattle since the Sonics left, Kerr showed up to his pregame press conference wearing a Sonics T-shirt.

At the time, he called the absence of the Sonics a real shame and said it was a black mark on the league. He also said the Sonics reminded him of the Warriors, with a cool brand, strong tradition and a passionate fan base.

Kerr has history with the franchise from his playing days, too. He was part of the Chicago Bulls team that beat the Sonics in six games in the 1996 NBA Finals, and he has fondly recalled the energy and noise inside KeyArena during that series.

Now in his 13th season as Golden State's head coach, Kerr has continued to back Seattle's push for a team whenever he has been asked.

Where Expansion Stands

Kerr's comments come at a key moment in Seattle's long wait.

In March 2026, the NBA Board of Governors voted unanimously to formally explore expansion to Seattle and Las Vegas. The vote did not guarantee teams for either city, but it kicked off the process of evaluating ownership groups, arenas and markets, with the 2028–29 season discussed as a target entry point.

Commissioner Adam Silver has said the league wants an answer on expansion by the end of 2026. He has also said expansion fees could run between $7 billion and $10 billion per franchise.

Seattle already has a ready-made home in Climate Pledge Arena, the renovated building on the site of the old KeyArena.

The Mexico City Factor

In recent months, though, the conversation has gotten more complicated.

ESPN's Brian Windhorst reported that Silver told team owners that Seattle was no longer a lock for an expansion franchise. Silver also raised the possibility of a team in Mexico City, where an ownership group has pitched a franchise and a new arena district.

Mexico City already has an NBA G League team, the Capitanes, and the league has played regular-season games there for years. With a metro population of more than 21 million, it is an attractive market for a league focused on international growth.

Still, many around the league view the Mexico City talk as a negotiating tactic. Raising the possibility of another city could push Seattle's prospective owners to improve their offers. Silver himself has described Mexico City as more of a possibility down the road, while saying the league is looking closely at returning to Seattle.

Seattle's History as Leverage

This would not be the first time Seattle's name has come up during negotiations elsewhere. Since the Sonics left for Oklahoma City in 2008, the city has often been mentioned as a possible destination when teams have pushed their local governments for new or renovated arenas, including in Phoenix.

For Sonics fans, that has been a frustrating pattern. Their city has been treated as a bargaining chip while they wait for a team of their own.

Kerr's comment that "business is business" acknowledged that reality without endorsing it.

Waiting for a Decision

Seattle had an NBA team from 1967 until 2008, when the Sonics relocated to Oklahoma City and became the Thunder. The franchise won the 1979 NBA championship and produced stars such as Gary Payton, Shawn Kemp and a rookie Kevin Durant.

Nearly two decades later, the city is closer than ever to getting its team back. A decision could come within weeks.

Whatever the league decides, Kerr has made his position clear. The Sonics belong in Seattle.
excerpt: Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr reiterated his long-standing support for Seattle's NBA expansion bid, saying "the Sonics belong in Seattle," as the league moves closer to a decision on expansion franchises for Seattle and Las Vegas.
